title: How was the predicted famine of the 1960s avoided?
subtitle: The Green Revolution
subject: histoire
description: In 1960, the whole world feared a planetary famine: the population was exploding and harvests could not keep up. It never came, thanks to new seeds and a little-known American agronomist.
author: myra-houser

hero.hook: In 1960, the world expected to starve. One agronomist and a few grains of wheat would defeat the prophecy.

blocks.text: The year **1960** was one of those dates when humanity braced for the worst. War, the first signs of climate change and new technologies that could spread fear in an instant all came together. One worry stood out: a famine was about to sweep the world. Farm yields were low, several regions of the globe were already going hungry, and the apocalyptic tone of the Cold War did not help.

The famines of those years were real, but far less widespread than predicted. In the meantime, technical advances had transformed the way food was grown, and then transported. This is the story of the [[Green Revolution]], of its successes in Mexico and India, and of the countries it did not save.

sections.title: From the Dust Bowl to the baby boom: the fear of running out

blocks.text: A famine is a widespread lack of food, and it usually leads to mass death. It grows out of farming that no longer pays, or out of a lack of planning. Stable societies know how to counter it through trade or stored reserves. But when the whole planet believes it is under threat, the response is far harder to organize.

blocks.caption: "Migrant Mother" by Dorothea Lange (1936): a family of farm laborers during the Great Depression.

blocks.text: In the late 1950s, many Americans still remembered the [[Dust Bowl]], the dust storms that ruined the farms of the Great Plains, and the Great Depression that began with the crash of **1929**. Both had brought hunger. Meanwhile, the world's population was growing fast in the 20th century, and faster still after the postwar [[baby boom]]. A fear took hold: traditional farming would not keep up, and farmers would not be able to feed the world.
The fear of 1960 spread through a brand-new medium: television. In front of the evening news, millions of households convinced themselves that a world famine was just around the corner.

sections.title: Norman Borlaug and the Green Revolution

blocks.text: The 1930s did not only produce the Dust Bowl. They also sowed the techniques that would avert the famines to come. In Mexico, the government launched the **MAP** program, for Mexican Agricultural Production, together with the [[Rockefeller Foundation]], a philanthropic organization based in the United States. An American agronomist worked there: [[Norman Borlaug]]. He developed varieties of corn and wheat that grew faster and adapted to different climates. Within ten years, Mexico was exporting wheat.

blocks.caption: Water from a tube well irrigating wheat in India, 1968: irrigation went hand in hand with the Green Revolution's seeds.

blocks.text: India, independent since **1947**, followed the same path. Borlaug worked there with government agronomists to introduce new seed varieties. Added to advances in irrigation and transport, these plants changed everything: many countries managed to feed themselves, and even to feed the people they exported to. The planetary famine predicted for 1960 never happened.
For this work, Norman Borlaug earned a nickname that stuck: the "Father of the Green Revolution."

sections.title: The famines that did happen: Biafra and China

blocks.text: Averting a famine depends first of all on a state's ability to distribute food aid. In 1960, not every country had the means, and many lived through a very different story from Mexico or India. In Nigeria, newly independent, the southern region of [[Biafra]] seceded in **1967**. The government blocked its access to the ports: nothing got in. The famine that followed was widely covered by the press. Its images of children with swollen bellies left a lasting mark and fixed durable stereotypes.

blocks.caption: Makeshift blast furnaces in the Chinese countryside during the Great Leap Forward, in 1958.

blocks.text: In China, the [[Great Leap Forward]] launched by Mao upended the way the state collected and redistributed grain. The first deaths came in **1958**. By 1962, nearly **50 million** people had died. Despite the successes of the Green Revolution elsewhere, the news from the countries that were hit remained devastating.

The Green Revolution continued into the **1980s**. It led to genetically modified crops, more resistant to drought and to pests and able to feed more people. Combined with the clearing of forests, they allowed many countries to feed their own populations.

blocks.text: In the 21st century, local food movements have questioned this method and pointed to the damage it may do to the environment. Writers such as **Barbara Kingsolver** and **Michael Pollan** have criticized the massive use of genetically modified crops, harmful in their view to the land and to the people who eat them. The Green Revolution kept the famine of 1960 at bay. Half a century later, its legacy draws as much praise as blame.

The world famine predicted for 1960 never came, thanks to Norman Borlaug's seeds and the Green Revolution, but famine did strike where the state could not or would not feed its people: in Biafra and in the China of the Great Leap Forward.
